content_html:
TCM × Boundaries × Schemas

Temporal Context Models explain continuity: a slowly drifting internal context binds nearby items and supports “recall neighbors.” Event segmentation explains discontinuity: prediction-error spikes trigger boundaries that reset the event model and separate episodes. Schemas bias the balance by reducing prediction error (fewer boundaries, faster consolidation) until mismatch forces an update.

Temporal Context Models (TCM/CMR)

Drifting context: Experience evolves an internal temporal state; each item binds to the current state, and retrieval reinstates it—cuing neighbors in time (contiguity, recency).

Reinstatement: Recalling one element partially restores its learned context, explaining serial clustering in free recall.

Event boundaries as context resets

Event Segmentation Theory: Perception uses prediction; when prediction error spikes (goal / scene / actor / time / causal shifts), an event boundary resets the event model.

Neural signatures: Hippocampal activity peaks at boundaries; cortex tracks event structure across nested timescales.

Behavioral pattern: Stronger within‑event than across‑boundary associations—consistent with a context jump at boundaries.

Schemas tilt the balance

Efficiency: When input fits an existing schema, encoding needs less binding and systems consolidation accelerates. Stability vs. updating: Schemas lower prediction error (fewer boundaries) until mismatch grows; then a boundary triggers updating or new schema formation.

Integrated picture

Continuity (TCM/CMR): slowly drifting temporal context binds neighbors. Discontinuity (Event segmentation): boundaries punctuate streams into episodes. Efficiency (Schemas): prior knowledge compresses congruent details, speeding consolidation and suppressing unnecessary boundaries.
